results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 53 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in spec order; no unit is unmatched.
The reverse outliner marked no unit as holding two ideas.
Every unit supports S1 (styles p13-p15), S2 (triggers p16-p19, p35), S3 (wiring p21-p28), S4 (trade-offs, per flow, stages), S5 (inventory, In Practice, failures) or frames/synthesizes the thesis.

results.draft_locus: Five Ways to Trigger an Exchange ¶1
results.quote: The table is the author's synthesis of the vendor documentation cited under "In Practice" and in the next chapter.
results.finding: The trigger table's source pointer is stale: the vendor documentation now sits in the next two paragraphs of this section (p17, p35, moved there in round 2), and In Practice cites no vendor documentation, so a reader who follows the pointer finds nothing (first flow reader, item 3.5).

Other evidence is explained where it appears: the Hohpe-Woolf and Gartner quotations, the Shopify, Stripe and Business Central documentation, the link arithmetic, the price points with the per-flow comparison at 950 orders a day, the inventory columns and excerpt, and each incident with its fix.

Every term on audience.does_not_know is explained at or before first use: integration style and the four styles, synchronous/asynchronous, queue and broker, polling, scheduled batch, CDC, event notification and event-carried state transfer, point to point, hub, vendor connector, iPaaS metering units, integration inventory and integration debt.
The introduction opens on the puzzling scenario of a lost or doubled order message, defines the term with the Black Friday case, states the two-part thesis and gives a roadmap; no weak pattern.
The conclusion answers the opening case with both halves and sorts the take-aways by how settled they are, then hands off; it does not merely restate or open a new topic.

p50 sets the order handoff against the per-flow style and the owner together and names where the incidents lacked one half; p53 and the questions turn it into the course of action (inventory with owners before any tool).
"The chapter opened with an order whose message to the warehouse is lost or arrives twice." p50 answers it with the webhook or event, polling sweep, idempotent receiver and owner.

The intro reader predicted every expected element: customer harm from a lost or doubled handoff, what an integration is and decides, styles, triggers and wiring with iPaaS cost, per-flow choice by needs and stage, the inventory and debt, Eva's order and the stock path, the failures, recovery and versioning left to linked chapters; evidence from Kestrel & Pine's 34 integrations, the Black Friday delay and vendor documentation.

The reader summed the hops to over two hours, gave 570 orders per fifteen minutes at 38 a minute, stock as events per SKU and location into an availability service with reconciliation and a safety buffer, orders by webhook with a polling sweep and duplicate-ignoring consumers, finance by nightly batch reconciled against the PSP payout report, and the inventory with a named owner per row as the first step.

The reader rejected the company-wide 'event-driven' claim and the guarantee, cited Shopify's eight retries over four hours, deletion after eight failures and 'isn't always guaranteed', duplicates and out-of-order deliveries, and added a polling sweep or reconciliation job, idempotent receivers and an alert when the flow goes quiet.

The reader placed the payoff where flows and builders make point to point unmanageable, usually at Omnichannel; compared vendors per flow at own volume because units differ; and said a hub gives no ownership and without owner, contract and reconciliation recreates the tangle in one place.
